summary: Sets out requirements for how Generalized MPLS (GMPLS) signaling should be used and extended to support Automatically Switched Optical Networks (ASON). It focuses on time-division multiplexed connections such as SONET/SDH and optical transport networks. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: GMPLS is the signalling that sets up connections in optical networks. This memo lists what that signalling has to be able to do so that the network can be controlled by software rather than by hand.

questions: what is ason in optical networks

subtitle: What Generalized MPLS signalling has to be able to do so that optical networks can be run by software.

tldr.problem: Automatically switched optical networks need signalling that can set up connections across several providers' domains, survive a control plane failure, and work with links that use different kinds of technology.
tldr.mechanism: The memo lists seven functions the Generalized MPLS signalling has to support, including soft permanent connections, the separation of calls from connections, restart after failure, label mapping and crankback, and then states the backward compatibility rules any extension must obey.
tldr.outcome: The requirements were written as design input for extensions to the GMPLS signalling specifications, rather than as a protocol in their own right.

facts.label: Reference points in the ASON model

today: RFC 4139 is an Informational memo published in July 2005, and the metadata records no obsoleting or updating RFC. It sets out requirements rather than defining new signaling messages, and it says it introduces no new security requirements to GMPLS signaling.

sections.title: What GMPLS And ASON Are
sections.content:
The Generalized Multi-Protocol Label Switching (GMPLS) suite of protocol specifications controls different switching technologies and different applications. It supports requesting time division multiplexing connections, including SONET and SDH, and Optical Transport Networks, and it has capabilities needed for Automatically Switched Optical Network control planes. Those capabilities include generic ones such as call and connection separation and more specific ones such as support for soft permanent connections.

This memo concentrates on the signaling side of the GMPLS suite. It describes the functional requirements needed to support ASON, which may lead to extensions to GMPLS signaling, and it also sets out requirements that pertain to backward compatibility. A terminology appendix defines the terms the document uses. Although the document uses the RFC 2119 keywords, it uses them to describe design requirements for protocol extensions rather than to describe a protocol implementation.
sections.plainLanguage: GMPLS is the signalling that sets up connections in optical networks. This memo lists what that signalling has to be able to do so that the network can be controlled by software rather than by hand.

sections.title: The ASON Model And Its Three Interfaces
sections.content:
The ASON architecture applies an automated control plane to support both call and connection management services. It is a reference architecture: it describes functional components, abstract interfaces and interactions, not protocols. It distinguishes three reference points, which are points of information exchange: the user-network interface (UNI) between a user, who is the service requester, and a service provider control domain; the external network-network interface (E-NNI) between two control domains; and the internal network-network interface (I-NNI) within one control domain.

The I-NNI and E-NNI interfaces sit between protocol controllers, and may or may not use physical transport links. The memo warns against assuming a one-to-one relationship between control plane interfaces and physical links, between control plane entities and transport plane entities, or between control plane identifiers and transport plane resources.

Because ASON does not restrict the protocols used elsewhere in a network, support for its functions must be independent of any particular choice of UNI, I-NNI or E-NNI, so that implementations can interwork. The memo provides signaling requirements for the distributed call and connection management of G.8080 inside a GMPLS control domain and between GMPLS control domains. It does not restrict the use of other protocols inside a domain or as an E-NNI or UNI, and interworking with non-GMPLS protocols is left to the interworking function and outside its scope. Any user-network interface that complies with the GMPLS RSVP-TE extensions is part of the GMPLS suite and must be supported by the ASON GMPLS signaling functionality.
sections.plainLanguage: The ASON model defines where signalling happens: between a customer and a provider, between two providers, and inside one provider's network. It is a framework, not a protocol, so the requirements have to work whatever protocol a provider chose.

sections.title: The Seven Functions The Signaling Must Support
sections.content:
The memo then lists what the signaling has to support: soft permanent connection capability, call and connection separation, call segments, extended restart capabilities during control plane failures, extended label association, crankback capability, and additional error cases. Each gets its own subsection with the requirements it implies.

Two rules shape all of them. First, end-to-end signaling should work across administrative boundaries, protocols within the network, and however connections are realized in each part of the network, which means ASON signaling requests have to map cleanly between GMPLS control domains and non-GMPLS ones. Second, the extensions have to be backward compatible.
sections.plainLanguage: Seven functions have to be supported: soft permanent connections, separating calls from connections, call segments, surviving a control plane failure, mapping labels, retrying around a blocked path, and reporting new kinds of error.

sections.title: Soft Permanent Connections, Calls And Call Segments
sections.content:
A soft permanent connection combines a permanent connection on the source side of the user's network, a permanent connection on the destination side, and a switched connection inside the network. An Element Management System or Network Management System typically asks the ingress node to set up the switched connection, which the ingress node then does with the distributed GMPLS signaling protocol. The end-to-end connection is created by associating the incoming interface of the ingress node with the switched connection, and the outgoing interface of the egress node with the same switched connection. In the memo's figure, the user's node A is connected to the provider's node B over link 1, the user's node Z to the provider's node Y over link 3, and an abstract link 2 connects B and Y; B and Y are the ingress and egress of the switched connection. Links 1 and 3 are provisioned, while link 2 is set up by the control plane, so the soft permanent connection is the stitching of the three.

Two requirements follow. The signaling must be able to indicate the outgoing link and label information used when setting up the destination provisioned connection, and because ASON networks span domains, it should also support indicating the service level requested for the soft permanent connection, with the source and destination signaling controller addresses used where both endpoints need to be known.

A call, in the ASON sense, is an association between endpoints that supports an instance of a service. It can be seen as a service between two end points, with several calls possible between them and several connections associated with each call. A call does not carry traffic; it builds the relationship by which later connections may be made. It may be associated with zero, one or multiple connections, and those connections may be of different types and may exist independently of each other. The memo gives three reasons the separation is useful: it lets a call control component be separate from the nodes that host the connections, it identifies the call initiator before the connection is made, which can reduce contention during resource reservation, and it handles several connections together, such as a working connection and a recovery connection belonging to the same call. To support it, the signaling should include a call identification mechanism and should allow end-to-end call capability exchange. A feasible call identifier may concatenate a globally unique fixed part, such as a country or carrier code, with an operator-specific part made of an access point code and a local identifier, though other formats have to be possible too.

Call segmentation applies when a call crosses several control domains. An end-to-end call may then consist of several call segments, each with one or more associated connections and possibly a different number of connections. The caller interacts with the called party through intermediate network call controllers at the control domain boundaries, and the capabilities of each segment are set by the policies at those reference points. The point of segments is to allow independent policy choices of signaling, concatenation, data plane protection and recovery in different domains.
sections.plainLanguage: A soft permanent connection is a provisioned link at each end, joined by a connection that the network sets up in software. A call is not a connection: it is the agreement between two users, and one call can carry several connections.

sections.title: Restart, Label Association, Crankback And Errors
sections.content:
The requirements for recovering from a control plane failure are strict. Any failure, single or multiple, of control channels or controllers, must not release established calls and connections, including the transport plane connections behind them. A recovered control entity must be able to recover the status of the calls and connections that existed before the failure, the connectivity information of its neighbours, and the association between each call and its connections. Calls and connections that were being set up should be released or continued, and those that were being released must be released.

Extended label association covers the case where the network between two GMPLS-capable nodes is not GMPLS-capable. A label describes the resources used on one link for a particular connection, and may name a timeslot, a wavelength, or a port or fibre. In ASON the same label value need not mean the same thing on different links. The memo's example has two GMPLS nodes, A and Z, connected across two non-GMPLS nodes, B and C. Node A's outgoing VC-4 timeslot 1, with label [1,0,0,0,0], may be mapped onto node B's outgoing VC-4 timeslot 6, with label [6,0,0,0,0], or onto node C's outgoing VC-4 timeslot 4, with label [4,0,0,0,0]. By the time Z receives the request from A, its own local label and timeslot no longer match what it was sent. The control plane should therefore use a label association mechanism to map the received label into a locally significant one, either by manual provisioning or by discovery. Where two nodes are directly connected no association is needed at all, because the implicit label structure gives a one-to-one mapping.

Crankback lets a failed setup request be retried on an alternate path that avoids the blocked link or node. The blocking resource must be identified and returned in the error response to the repair node, the repair node computes an alternate path that satisfies the original constraints, and the setup request is re-initiated from the repair node. The memo expects the entity computing the new path to keep the identifiers of the blocking resources until the connection is established or the node gives up, and to keep the history of all blockages so that the next path computation avoids them. The number of retries should be strictly limited, either per connection or per node; when a node's limit is exceeded it reports the error upstream and its crankback information must say that rerouting through it will not succeed, and when the limit for a connection is exceeded the repair node sends an error upstream saying the maximum number of reroutings is exceeded.

The final group of requirements adds error cases for the ASON network: errors for basic call and soft permanent connection support, such as a wrong identifier for a call or an invalid interface identifier; errors for policy failure while processing new call and soft permanent connection capabilities, such as an unauthorized request; and errors for an incorrect service level.
sections.plainLanguage: A control plane failure must not tear down working connections. Labels may mean different things on different links, so the network needs a way to map one to another. And when a setup request hits a blocked path, the error must name the block so the request can be retried around it.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility And Security
sections.content:
Any extension to the GMPLS signaling protocol made for these requirements must be backward compatible. That means that in a network where some nodes support the extensions and some do not, it must still be possible to set up conventional connections between any pair of nodes across any set of nodes, and that using the extensions must not disturb the conventional connections that already exist.

Two further cases follow. When transit nodes that take no part in the new functions lie on the path of a call or connection, the extensions must let them pass the setup information on unmodified. And when a transit or egress node is asked to support a function it does not support, the extensions must allow the request to be rejected by pre-existing GMPLS mechanisms in a way that is not harmful to the network as a whole.

On security, the memo notes that it is not possible to establish a connection before call setup completes, and that policy and authentication procedures are applied before the call is established and may also be restricted to connection establishment within that call. It introduces no new security requirements to GMPLS signaling.
sections.plainLanguage: Old and new nodes have to coexist. A network that mixes them must still be able to set up ordinary connections, and a node that does not understand a new function must be able to say so safely.

viz.caption: THE SEVEN FUNCTIONS TO SUPPORT (RFC 4139 SECTION 3)

items.title: Soft permanent connection
items.text: A permanent connection at each end, stitched together by a switched connection in the network.

items.title: Call and connection separation
items.text: A call is the relationship between two users; the connections carry the traffic.

items.title: Call segments
items.text: An end-to-end call that crosses several control domains may be made of several segments.

items.title: Extended restart
items.text: A control plane failure must not release established calls and connections.

items.title: Extended label association
items.text: Map a label received from a neighbour into a locally significant one.

items.title: Crankback
items.text: Retry a failed setup request on a path that avoids the blocked link or node.

items.title: Additional error cases
items.text: Errors for wrong identifiers, policy failures and incorrect service levels.
